label: Unit 1
themeSub: How a machine learns, and what it can't do
intro: He is going to grow up with these things answering him, so the useful thing to install now isn't how to use one — it's that it guesses. A smart machine learns from examples, gets better with practice, is wrong sometimes, and is not alive no matter how much it sounds like it is. Two of the games here are about who to ask: some questions belong to a computer, and some belong to a person who loves you.

gelds.text: Says a computer guesses rather than knows
Knows a thing that talks or moves is not therefore alive
Says out loud that a machine can be wrong, and checks
Knows which questions go to a grown-up instead of a screen
Can describe learning as: examples, guess, correction, better

tryNote: The guessing game is the one that does the work — he plays the machine, which is the fastest way to feel why examples matter.

daily.title: You be the guessing machine
daily.do: You think of an animal. He gets to ask questions and then guess. When he's wrong you say "no, guess again" — never the answer. Point out what he did: he used what he'd already seen to make a better guess.
daily.stretch: Swap. He picks, you guess out loud badly on purpose, and he has to say why your guess was wrong. Explaining somebody else's mistake is harder than making your own.
daily.skill: Guessing from examples, and saying why

daily.title: Ask it, then check it
daily.do: When a speaker or a phone answers something in front of him, say out loud: "Let's check." Then check it, in the real world if you can. He should see grown-ups not taking a machine's word for it.
daily.stretch: Get him to say what he'd do if it was wrong. Ask a person, look in a book, go and see. Having somewhere else to go is the whole point.
daily.skill: A machine's answer is a start, not the end

daily.title: Alive, or just moves?
daily.do: Name things around the house and ask alive or not alive. The vacuum that drives itself, the cat, the talking speaker, the plant on the sill.
daily.stretch: Ask what makes the difference. Not the answer you'd write down — his. Grows, eats, gets hungry, can be hurt. Then tell him the speaker can't be any of those, however friendly it sounds.
daily.skill: Alive is not the same as acts alive

goalsTitle: What he should have by the end of this unit

his: Says a computer guesses, and can be wrong
Sorts alive from not alive, including things that move on their own
Knows the four steps: show it examples, it guesses, we correct it, it gets better
Comes to a person for the questions that need one
Isn't frightened of any of it — this is a tool, and he's the one holding it

weekend: Show him an image generator making something silly he asked for, once, with you sitting there. Then ask him what it got wrong. That question is the whole unit and it's the habit worth having.

songs.title: The Guessing Machine
songs.style: A gentle, curious preschool sing-along with soft toy-synth bleeps, ukulele and marimba. Slow, steady tempo a four-year-old can sing with, one warm friendly voice, a simple repeated melody, every word clear. Singing starts within the first two seconds, and it ends cleanly with no long outro.
lyrics: It learned from what we showed it,
It's not alive, it's not alive,
It doesn't feel, it doesn't sleep,
it does what it was taught.
When I have a big question
and the answer must be true,
I go and ask a person —
a real live person, like you!

advanced.label: Example
advanced.note: An example is one thing you show it. Show it a hundred cats and it learns cat.

advanced.label: Guess
advanced.note: A computer doesn't know. It makes its best guess.

advanced.label: Mistake
advanced.note: Computers make mistakes too. That is why we check.

advanced.label: Practice
advanced.note: The more examples it sees, the better its guesses get. Same as you.

advanced.label: Prompt
advanced.note: A prompt is what you ask it to do. Say it clearly and you get more back.

advanced.label: Sensor
advanced.note: A sensor is how a machine sees or hears. It's the machine's eyes.

advanced.label: Answer
advanced.note: An answer is what it gives back. It's a guess that sounds sure of itself.

advanced.label: Check
advanced.note: A check is finding out for real. Ask a person, open a book, go and look.

sort.title: Alive or Not Alive?
sort.noSay: Right. That one is not alive.
sort.retry: Does it grow? Does it get hungry? Have another go.

items.note: It eats, it grows, it gets tired. Alive.
It gets hot when we tell it to and that's all.
It grows and it drinks. Slowly, but it does.
You can love it and it is still not alive.
Small, and just as alive as the dog.
It goes because a person makes it go.
You grow every single day, even when you can't tell.

items.text: A vacuum that drives around the room by itself.
items.note: It moves on its own and it's still a machine. Moving isn't living.

items.text: A speaker that talks back when you ask it something.
items.note: It sounds like a person. It doesn't feel anything at all.

items.text: A seed in a cup of dirt.
items.note: It looks like nothing. It's alive and waiting.

items.text: A robot dog that wags its tail.
items.note: It was built to look happy. It can't be happy.
Alive, and it would rather be outside.
It walks until it runs down. Nothing in there wants anything.
It breathes the water. Alive.
It eats, and it flies off when it wants to.

items.text: A phone that says your name.
items.note: It says your name because somebody typed it in. It doesn't know you.

items.text: A pumpkin growing on a vine.
items.note: Still growing. Cut it off and it stops.
The dog was alive. The paper never was.

sort.title: Who Should You Ask?
sort.yesSay: Yes. A computer can help with that one.
sort.noSay: Right. That one is for a grown-up.
sort.retry: Think about who really knows the answer to that.

items.note: Facts like that are what a computer is good for.

items.text: Am I allowed to have a cookie?
items.note: Only the people who live with you can decide that.

items.text: What is the biggest animal in the ocean?
items.note: A computer has read more about whales than anybody in this house.
You'd have to look at your friend's face. A computer can't.
Never a screen for that one. Come and find a person.

items.text: How many legs does a spider have?
items.note: Eight, and a computer will say eight.

items.text: What should I do when I feel scared?
items.note: It can list ideas. It can't sit with you, and that's the part that helps.

items.text: What noise does a whale make?
items.note: It can even play it for you.

items.text: Should I be friends with that kid?
items.note: It doesn't know either of you. Ask somebody who does.

items.text: How do you say hello in Spanish?
items.note: Hola. Languages are a good job for a computer.

items.text: Is it okay to keep this a secret from Mom and Dad?
items.note: That question always comes to us. Always.

items.text: How tall is the tallest mountain?
items.note: A number nobody has to remember any more.
A body question goes to a person who can look at you.
A joey. Ask it, then tell me — I want to know if it's right.
Leaves off the tops of trees. Ask it, then we'll find a giraffe in a book and check.
That one comes to us, and the answer is yes. Always.
It reads the day off its clock. Ask it, then say it back to us so we can check.

items.text: Can I go to Grandma's house?
items.note: Only a grown-up in this house can say yes to that.

sets.goal: Teaching a computer what a cat is

steps.text: Show it lots of pictures of cats
We tell it if it was right
Check if the answer looks right
Ask a grown-up if you're not sure
Look it up in a book
Tell a grown-up what you found
Hold the treat up over its nose
Give it the treat when it sits
It sits when you say sit
